Dear Secretary Reese:

        Pursuant to Section 157.21(b) of the regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), LED Enterprises, LLC, an affiliate of Grupo CLISA
(hereafter referred to as “LED Enterprises”), submitted a request for approval to initiate the Pre-
Filing Process for the proposed Yuma Pipeline Project (“Project”) on March 19, 2025. On April
2, 2025, the Director of the Office of Energy Projects approved the Pre-Filing Request for the
Project.

         In accordance with the Commission’s regulations at 18 C.F.R. § 157.21(f)(5), LED
Enterprises submitted a draft of Resource Report 1 and Resource Report 10 for its Project on May
2, 2025, and a revised draft Resource Report 1 updated to reflect a route revision on March 26,
2026.
         LED Enterprises hereby submits updated drafts of Resource Reports 1 and 10, as well as
initial drafts of Resource Reports 2 through 9, and Resource Report 12.

        LED Enterprises requests that, pursuant to Section 388.112 of the Commission’s
regulations, certain stakeholder and landowner, and cultural resource information included in the
filing be treated as privileged and confidential (“PRIV”) and not be released to the public. This
type of information is customarily treated as privileged and confidential. Accordingly, these files
are labeled “CUI//PRIV.”
 September 28, 2026
Page 2

10. RESOURCE REPORT 10 – ALTERNATIVES
        LED Enterprises, LLC, an affiliate of Grupo CLISA (hereafter referred to as LED Enterprises),
is seeking a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (Certificate) under Section 7(c) of the
Natural Gas Act, a Presidential Permit for the border-crossing facilities, and a Natural Gas Act Section
3 authorization for the siting, construction, and operation of the Yuma Pipeline Project (Project).
        The proposed Project will consist of approximately 138 miles of new 30-inch diameter pipeline
and related facilities to be located in Maricopa and Yuma counties, Arizona, designed to transport up
to 800 million cubic feet per day (MMcf/d) of natural gas from an interconnection with an existing
pipeline to the United States (U.S.)/Mexico border near San Luis, Arizona. LED Enterprises expects to
begin construction of the Project in Q1 2028 and to place the Project in service in Q4 2028.
       As part of the development of the Project, LED Enterprises evaluated multiple route options in
conjunction with the guidance set forth in 18 Code of Federal Regulations Section 380.12.
Alternatives considered include the no action alternative, system alternatives, pipeline alternatives
(major and minor route alternatives), and aboveground facility alternatives.
       Evaluation criteria utilized to select the preferred alternative included:

       •        Ability to meet the purpose and need of the Project;

       •        Technical feasibility and practicality; and

       •        Significant environmental advantage over the proposed action.

        This revised draft Resource Report 10 describes the various alternatives considered for the
Project.

10.1 PURPOSE AND NEED

        As described in Resource Report 1 – Project Description, the purpose of the Project is to
transport up to 800 MMcf/d natural gas to supply the new demand for power generation, industrial,
residential consumption, and other new demands in the northwestern Mexican market, as well as the
demand for power generation in the Yuma area and throughout Arizona. Thus, the Project is
specifically designed to increase access of natural gas from the U.S. market to customers located in
northwest Mexico and the Yuma, Arizona area.
        Baja California State of Mexico (Baja California) lacks its own natural gas production, has a
separate power grid than the rest of Mexico, and relies entirely on imports from the U.S. The primary
transportation pipeline in the U.S. that transports domestic natural gas into Baja California through
various border crossings is the El Paso Natural Gas (EPNG) via the North Baja Pipeline. The North
Baja Pipeline delivers the gas to Gasoducto Rosarito Pipeline at the U.S./Mexico border which
transports the gas into Baja California. These pipelines are fully subscribed and there is a need for
additional capacity to supply additional natural gas to support the growing economy (The Institute of
Americas, 2022).



Revised Draft                                  10-1                                    September 2026
                                                                                   Yuma Pipeline Project
                                                          Revised Draft Resource Report 10—Alternatives
        In addition to supplying growing natural gas demand in Baja California, the Project is also
designed to transport natural gas to the growing market in Yuma, Arizona area. Approximately half of
the total capacity of the Project (400 MMcf/d) will be available to the Yuma area. Yuma has also
experienced significant population growth within the city and surrounding county over the past four
decades. The population has more than doubled from 42,433 in 1980 to 101,964 in 2024 (City of
Yuma, 2024). This growing population in an arid environment prone to high temperatures leads to
higher demand for energy sources to provide reliability (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2024).

10.2 NO-ACTION ALTERNATIVE

       Under the no-action alternative, Project construction and operation would not occur, and
environmental impacts directly related to the construction and operation of the Project would not occur.
The no-action alternative would not accomplish the Project’s objectives of supplying natural gas via
the EPNG Pipeline to an interconnect in Mexico for the market needs in Baja California, as well as the
Yuma County region.
       As described in Section 10.1, there is a growing demand for natural gas in Baja California and
Yuma, Arizona. If this Project is not constructed, it is likely that a similar project will be required to fill
the need. LED Enterprises has assessed the potential alternatives for meeting the regional need, and
the proposed Project is the most logical solution to meet the demand that has the least environmental
impacts and is the most practicable of the alternatives considered.
        The no-action alternative does not meet the purpose and need of the Project; thus, the no-
action alternative was not accepted.

10.3 NON-GAS ENERGY ALTERNATIVES

       The Project’s purpose is to provide up to 800 MMcf/d natural gas to the northwestern Mexican
market, as well as to the Yuma area in Arizona. A non-gas energy alternative will not meet the
purpose and need for the Project.

10.4 SYSTEM ALTERNATIVES

       System alternatives consist of existing natural gas facilities, pipelines, or alternate existing
configurations of facilities that would meet the purpose and need of the Project without constructing
the Project. System alternatives also involve the transportation of the equivalent amount of
incremental natural gas volumes by the expansion of existing pipeline systems.
        LED Enterprises assessed existing and proposed natural gas transportation facilities in the
region including the existing North Baja Pipeline and the proposed Desert Southwest Expansion
Project, as shown in Figure 10-1, Appendix 10A.

10.4.1 System Alternative A – Existing North Baja Pipeline

      Baja California is currently served through the existing North Baja Pipeline (north of
U.S./Mexico border) and the Gasoducto Rosarito Pipeline (south of U.S./Mexico border). These



Revised Draft                                    10-2                                        September 2026
                                                                                  Yuma Pipeline Project
                                                         Revised Draft Resource Report 10—Alternatives
pipelines have the capability to transport approximately 500 MMcf/d of natural gas. The North Baja
Pipeline is currently building an expansion to increase its capacity to around 1.0 billion cubic feet per
day. This expansion will be dedicated to a liquified natural gas plant that is being built in Ensenada,
Mexico. With this expansion, the North Baja Pipeline will be near maximum capacity. For additional
expansions, there will be a need to build new compressor stations in California to add more capacity.
The North Baja Pipeline could not meet the Project’s purpose and need without significant expansion
and additional compression, which would result in similar or greater environmental and landowner
impacts as the Project. Therefore, the North Baja Pipeline does not represent a reasonable system
alternative.

10.4.2 System Alternative B – Proposed Desert Southwest Expansion Project

         Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (Transwestern) is owned by Energy Transfer and
consists of multiple natural gas transmission pipelines across Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona.
Currently, Transwestern is in the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Pre-filing Process
for the Desert Southwest Expansion Project. The purpose of the Desert Southwest Expansion Project
is to transport approximately 2.3 billion cubic feet per day from the Permian Basin to customers in New
Mexico and Arizona, and to upgrade Transwestern’s existing Phoenix Lateral to allow bi-directional
flow. This alternative would require the construction of approximately 150 miles of new pipeline from
the existing and proposed Transwestern system. The available capacity of the Transwestern system
is unknown. One of the primary customers the Project is intending to serve does not have capacity on
the Transwestern system; however, they do have transportation capacity on the EPNG system that
they utilize and optimize every day from the Permian/Waha receipt points to the different delivery
points along the El Paso South Mainline. The proposed Desert Southwest Expansion could not meet
the Project’s purpose and need without significant expansion and additional compression, which would
result in similar or greater environmental and landowner impacts as the Project. Therefore, the
Proposed Desert Southwest Expansion Project does not represent a reasonable system alternative.

       •        Minimizes construction within mountainous regions;

       •        Avoids or minimize effects on scenic areas, historic properties, wildlife, and recreational
                values;

       •        Is collocated with existing utility or transportation rights-of-way (ROW), where practical;

       •        Avoids designated critical habitats, National Wildlife Refuges, and officially designated

10.5.1.1 Preferred Route

        The Preferred Route is approximately 138.1 miles long and crosses Yuma and Maricopa

infrastructure for approximately 101.3 miles, or 73 percent. The Preferred Route avoids the
mountainous terrain in the surrounding environment.
        The Preferred Route crosses approximately 1,007.7 acres of private land, 773.8 acres of
federal land, and 310.3 acres of state land. Of the public lands crossed, the Preferred Route crosses
approximately 514.2 acres of Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land (25 percent of total ROW),

       The Preferred Route was designed to avoid mountainous terrain, enabling a more efficient
construction schedule for the Project with less blasting, reduced costs, and improved accessibility.

10.5.1.2 Alternative Route A

       Alternative Route A is approximately 131.8 miles long and follows the Preferred Route except
for approximately 35 miles on the southern extent near the U.S./Mexico border. Similar to the
Preferred Route, this route also avoids mountainous slopes in the surrounding region. Approximately
91.8 miles, or 70 percent of this route is collocated with existing utilities.
       Alternative Route A crosses approximately 824.6 acres of private land, 902.1 acres of federal
land, and 270.3 acres of state land. Of the public lands crossed, Alternative Route A crosses
approximately 523.4 acres of BLM land (26 percent of total ROW), 212.5 acres of BOR land
(11 percent), 166.1 acres of Barry M. Goldwater Range land (8 percent), and 0.2 acre of IBWC
property (less than 1 percent).
       Alternative Route A has the least amount of collocation available. It also crosses more federal
land than the Preferred Route, including U.S. Air Force land associated with military airports. Due to
the federal land crossed by the route and reduced collocation opportunities, this alternative was
dismissed.

10.5.1.3 Alternative Route B

       Alternative Route B is approximately 91.8 miles long and crosses Yuma and La Paz Counties,
Arizona. Alternative Route B would tie into EPNG Pipeline near Quartzsite, Arizona, and travel south
to Yuma, Arizona. This route parallels Interstate 95 and crosses the Yuma Proving Ground and the
Kofa National Wildlife Refuge. Alternative Route B is collocated with existing utilities and ROWs for
approximately 68.8 miles (74 percent).
       Alternative Route B crosses approximately 253.6 acres of private land, 1,027.8 acres of federal
land, and 108.6 acres of state land, including a wildlife refuge. Of the public lands crossed, Alternative
Route B crosses approximately 490.3 acres of BLM-managed land (35 percent of total ROW), 167.5
acres of BOR-managed land (12 percent), 369.8 acres of Yuma Test Range land (27 percent), and
0.2 acre of IBWC property (less than 1 percent).
         Alternative Route B has the least potential impact through the reduced mileage required and
the greatest percentage of collocation opportunities. Similar to the Preferred Route, the location of
this alternative offers additional optionality for potential take-off points in the surrounding Yuma area.
Alternative Route B also has the greatest number of federal lands crossed including the U.S. Army
Yuma Proving Ground (or Yuma Test Range) and the Kofa Wildlife Refuge.
      Due to the location through the Yuma Proving Ground and Kofa Wildlife Refuge, Alternative
Route B was not selected as the preferred alternative.

10.5.1.4 Alternative Route C

       Alternative Route C is approximately 138.3 miles long and crosses Yuma and Maricopa
Counties, Arizona. Alternative Route C is similar to the Preferred Route from Milepost (MP) 0.0 to
MP 71.4, where it deviates from the preferred route and is generally collocated with the Union Pacific
Railroad for approximately 40 miles before rejoining the preferred route near MP 110.9. Alternative
Route C is collocated with existing utilities and ROW for approximately 122.0 miles (88 percent).
       Alternative Route C crosses approximately 1,061.6 acres of private land, 763.9 acres of federal
land, and 275.5 acres of state land. Of the public lands crossed, Alternative Route C crosses
approximately 468.3 acres of BLM-managed land (22 percent of total ROW), 295.5 acres of BOR-
managed land (14 percent), and 0.2 acre of IBWC property (less than 1 percent). Unlike Alternative
Routes A and B, this route does not cross any military-managed lands (e.g., Barry M. Goldwater
Range or Yuma Test Range).
       Alternative Route C offers the greatest collocation opportunity and the least federal land
crossed of the alternatives evaluated, and avoids the military installations crossed by Alternative
Routes A and B. However, this route crosses the most private land and the most farmland of unique
importance of any route, which may indicate increased impacts to local landowners and farmers.
       Due to the increased impact to private landowners and agriculture, Alternative Route C was not
selected as the preferred alternative.

         From approximately MP 102.9 to MP 103.3, LED Enterprises evaluated and incorporated an
